cues.text: Suspicion at the Heart of the Court

The Roman historian Tertullian remembered Domitian as a man who inherited a portion of Nero's own cruelty, and by the final years of his reign (AD 81–96) that cruelty had turned decisively against the Christians of the empire.
Unlike Nero's persecution, confined largely to the city of Rome in the aftermath of the Great Fire, Domitian's suspicion reached into the very heart of the imperial court itself.
Tertullian, writing a century later, drew a sharp distinction between the two.
Nero's fury had been the wild cruelty of a monster.
Domitian pursued his persecution with colder, more calculating malice, seeking out enemies real and imagined among Romans closest to his throne.
Martyrs of Consular Rank
Among the most notable victims of what the early Church remembered as its Second Persecution were figures of genuine political standing.
These included Flavius Clemens , a former consul and the emperor's own cousin, and Manius Acilius Glabrio , likewise a former consul.

Both were condemned, according to the ancient historian Dio Cassius, on charges of "atheism," the standard Roman accusation against those who abandoned the state religion for what officials regarded as a strange and dangerous foreign superstition.
An Apostle Exiled to Patmos
The most enduring memory of this persecution belongs to the Apostle John .
Ancient and consistent tradition places him in exile on the small Aegean island of Patmos during Domitian's reign's final year.
Irenaeus recorded this tradition, having himself known John's own disciple Polycarp; Eusebius and Jerome repeated it.
John was banished, in his own words, "on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus."
A Revelation Written in Exile
It was on this same barren island, tradition holds, that John received the extraordinary visions that would become the Book of Revelation.
They formed a message of hope and ultimate victory, composed remarkably in the very moment and place of the empire's attempt to silence its author.
We recognize here a pattern the Church would see again and again: that no exile, however remote, has ever succeeded in separating a faithful witness from the flock still listening for his voice.
No detail of that private vision reaches us untouched by nineteen centuries of retelling.
Yet the core memory has never wavered: a lonely exile, and a message of ultimate hope smuggled out from beneath the very shadow of the throne that had sent him there.
A Sudden End
Domitian's persecution ended as abruptly as it had begun: assassinated in a palace conspiracy on September 18, AD 96, he was succeeded by the elderly senator Nerva.
Nerva discontinued the persecution and recalled the exiles — among them, by the Church's ancient memory, John himself, who returned at last to resume his ministry at Ephesus.
Legacy
The persecution under Domitian remains a sober reminder that imperial hostility toward the Church was never confined to a single unstable tyrant.
It could resurface, a generation later, in a ruler determined to root out even the small handful of Christians close enough to his own throne to reach.
Yet the very island meant to silence the Church's last living Apostle became the place where he received and set down one of Scripture's most enduring visions of hope.
This proved that a persecuting empire's reach, however wide, has never once matched the reach of the word it tried to suppress.
We recognize in this pattern something the Church has seen repeated across every century since: persecution rarely announces itself as a single, isolated storm.
Instead, it returns generation after generation, wearing whatever face the current ruler's own fears and suspicions happen to give it.
Every later century of Christian exile and imprisonment has, in some measure, retraced this same pattern first set on Patmos: a body confined, a voice set free.
